batchName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE) - Latin words
chapterName: Late Republic: Cicero, Catiline and the Triumvirate (63-53 BCE)
description: Written by hand from the chapter text: the Latin words it explains

questions.question: After the conspiracy, senators hailed Cicero as pater patriae. What does it mean?
questions.explanation: He had just announced the executions with a single word: vixerunt.
questions.sourceQuote: Senators hailed him as "father of the fatherland" (*pater patriae*).

questions.question: At Carrhae the Parthians captured the legions’ aquilae. What were they?
options: The sacred eagles, the legions’ standards
questions.explanation: About 20,000 Romans died and 10,000 were captured.
questions.sourceQuote: along with the legions' sacred eagles (*aquilae*).

questions.question: What did Caesar give up in 60 BC so he could stand for consul?
options: A triumphus, the grand victory parade
questions.explanation: His enemies then saddled him with a hostile fellow consul.
questions.sourceQuote: gave up a triumph (*triumphus*), the grand victory parade every general craved, so he could stand for consul.

questions.question: How did Cicero announce the executions, with the word vixerunt?
questions.explanation: The five conspirators had been strangled.
questions.sourceQuote: Cicero announced it with a single grim word, "they have lived" (*vixerunt*), meaning they were dead.

questions.question: After Catiline joined the rebel army, the Senate declared him a hostis. What did that mean?
questions.explanation: It then sent Cicero’s fellow consul to fight him.
questions.sourceQuote: The Senate declared him a public enemy (*hostis*)

questions.question: What was Caesar’s lex agraria of 59 BC for?
options: Settling Pompey’s veterans and poor citizens on land
Giving Caesar a command in Gaul
questions.explanation: A conservative senator talked endlessly to block it, and Caesar took it to the people.
questions.sourceQuote: He drafted a carefully balanced land law (*lex agraria*) to settle Pompey's veterans and poor citizens

questions.question: How long had it been since any of Catiline’s ancestors was one of the consules?
questions.explanation: Catiline stood for the consulship again and again and was rejected every time.
questions.sourceQuote: None of his ancestors had held the consulship, Rome's top office, shared each year by two consuls (*consules*), for some four centuries.

questions.question: Who blocked Cicero’s farewell speech at the end of his consulship?
questions.explanation: Tribunes were armed with a veto; one tried to prosecute Cicero for killing citizens without trial.
questions.sourceQuote: two tribunes of the plebs (*tribuni plebis*), officials elected to protect ordinary citizens and armed with a veto, blocked his farewell speech.
